items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: they have to hear older stuff too: James P. Johnson, Teddy Wilson, that would be enough to start with.

ctx.x: Okay. Well then they ought to hear the greatest jazz pianist, who is Art Tatum. I would say they have to hear Art Tatum, they have to hear Oscar Peterson of course, and they have to hear Bill Evans, and they have to hear older stuff too: James P. Johnson, Teddy Wilson, that would be enough to start with. And that’s of course in addition to what I imagine such people would already be interested in, I assume that they would know all about Chick Corea and Herbie Hancock and people more recent even than those two.…

As a jazz musician through the years, what was your take on what was happening in the real popular field. When Elvis came on the scene and all that, today’s jazz musician looks at the things, you know the rap is happening and Madonna and that kind of thing. Back then did you have an interest in that kind of music that was coming along, I mean —

items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I went back and re-learned “Carolina Shout” from Johnson’s original recording

ctx.x: So much for predictions. They did re-issue that and the following James P. Johnson album as one CD which is now available. But now I think even that’s been cut out.
Oh. It’s a great sound. There’s some challenging parts in there too.
